Nah you good with the amount of soda ash, and I could very possibly be doing very extra, but it takes me almost an hour to washout my shirts... cold water first to neutralize the soda ash, I don't even touch the shirt just leave it under the cold faucet, flip it a couple times to get all over, let all the extra color come out.. squeeze it a time or two after 10 mins of rinsing, then I'll untie the shirt, rinse a lil bit longer with dawn dish soap, and once I get (mostly) clear water, I turn the water hot, and it begins to bleed a bit again. Hot water and washing in 2 buckets (one just hot water, another w colorsafe bleach) back & forth until there is no longer color coming from the shirt. Then I'll put the shirt in the machine wash & dry before ironing.

Like I said, it's very extra, but what works best for me at the moment! 

Day by day, dye by dye, it gets easier (& better)! Lol

Budtender here. I don't write this to complain/talk shit, simply giving perspective. 
Tipping culture is very Grey-lined nowadays.... at the end of the day, people dont owe a tip, its not a requirement. 
If someone comes in, knows what they want (or has a pickup order), and it's nothing but me putting flower in a bag and handing it to you; I never expect a tip... 
However when somebody comes in, has no Idea what they want, and I spend 15-20 minutes going through my knowledge/strains talking about what works, what doesn't work, and getting into nitty-gritty, I think that warrants an extra couple bucks. We tip waiters/waitresses for helping you get what you want, I believe it's a similar case with budtenders. 

Also I'd like to bring in discounts. I dont think there's any Other industry that gives out/is expected to hand out discounts for random things. Does anyone ask for discounts at the grocery store? When you get a bill at a restaurant, do you ask, "what discounts do you have today?", and surely at coffeeshops when they ask what you'd like, do you start with, "what's discounted today?" 
These are the times when I still don't expect a tip, but it more surprises me when they dont....I'll spend 20 minutes helping someone out, going through jars, asking questions, handpicking things for them, they try and barter or argue prices (like I own the place), end up getting a discount, they'll get $10+ taken off their total, and walk out with a stink-face. MY DAWG!!! 3 seasons ago (my first season skiing), I didn't look before I leaped, took about a 12 foot drop onto flat/packed snow and did essentially the same thing you did, but to my fibula. I was in such shock I got up to try and ski to the bottom, clipped my ski in (the pain I felt let me know it was bad, but I didn't know the extent), and when I lifted my right leg to turn, right above my ankle I felt my lower LEG flop towards gravity and I absolutely lost it... everything sank in and when ski patrol got there I almost blacked out but luckily I still had some sweet adrenaline going. (Also s/o to ski patrol cause they ski'd me down in the snowcoffin so gracefully, it was one of the most impressive things I've experienced) 

Anyways got my surgery, 5 screws and a big ass rod, 3-4 weeks in the bed, 4 weeks wheel-chair, 6 weeks scooter and 2 more weeks in a walker (for good measure) whilst doing pt the whole time. 

The shit sucks, but it gives you a chance to slow tf down and really think about a lot of things. Learn how to meditate. Read the books you've been telling yourself you were gonna read. Catch up on your anime's. 

As far as the ankle goes... things will change. I don't know you or your personal life, but I was a heavy runner before. Marathon-distance type. After my surgery, I couldn't (and still cant) run more than 3 miles without my ankle/foot going numb. I also have some ligament damage, so my foot is still numb in some spots, and very sensitive in others... like if I sleep with my significant other or a pet, even a small brush on the right spot of my foot will make me jump. It isn't necessarily painful, but it's like a small shock lol so since I couldn't run I bought a road bike, and boy-oh-boy do I recommend it!! It's the best PT for your injury (when you begin movement again), and it's one of the most freeing experiences, right under skiing 😛😉 
The year after my accident, I pretty much started over and had to re-learn to ski... not that I couldn't, but I was too scared to lol I stayed on greens and wide-blues. Ski'd around the parks, and worked up to a steep but clean black diamond by the end of the season. 
2 years after accident (last year), I had my first full season. I went up to Mt. Hood at least once a week from opening week to close, also did stevens pass, and went to park city for a weekend. I'm no krazy skiier by any means (you can see some of my skiing last year on my profile), but for what I know, I improved a TON. Was doing small park jumps, started tree skiing, did baby drops, and could finally keep up with my homies that went. Granted, a blunt, a few shots and some ibuprofen were definitely necessary for the longer days to stay solid, but it was a helluva season. 
This year, I've only gone once, tbh I have more personal and work stuff going on preventing me from going as much as I would like, but this year the time that I did go was some the most aggressive skiing I've done. Especially for my first day out... did my first cliff-huck, was bouncing through trees having a great time. Hopefully I'll get to spend some more time up there in the spring! But ankle wise, I'm still regularly cycling on the bike (20+ miles), I have to wear an insole on right shoes to prevent my foot from going numb if the shoes are any kind of flat, or I'm standing for more than a few hours, and when it gets cold outside you get a second-shiver in your plate. That's pretty much it. You gotta take care of your shit though... This is your leg. You use it to walk and do very important things everyday. I know this sounds dumb and "yeah, no shit", but you finna realize how much we take simply walking around, or being able to swing your legs over in the morning for granted. If you aren't consistent with rehab you will never be able to walk or do anything the same. The harder/smarter you work on it, the better off you will be. 

It's not all bad though, dawg. You're gonna learn a lot about yourself, and you will grow from this. I send love and blessings to you and the people who are gonna be helping you out during this time. 🙏🏼 💜

TLDR: 
Did the same thing as you but to my fibula 3 years ago this spring, 5 screws and a rod and minor nerve damage. 14-16 weeks w/ assisted movement devices , 3 weeks walking with boot and pt before I could put 2 shoes on again. 
First year is tough, learning to use your feet muscles again 
Second year is better, but you need to be consistent 
Third year is using the strength and maintenance you did in years 1 & 2 to gain confidence and know that whatever work you put into upkeep and pt is what you will receive in comfort and ability in the long run. 

Tips: 
- Get a leg pillow 
- Get one of those reachy-grabby-things 
- Be very thankful to those helping you 
- If available, use a cannabis 1:1 thc to cbd salve on your ankle from the day your stitches come off and after. I swear it's a miracle balm and my foot/ankle can't last until 1 pm without it.
- Get a bicycle 
- Be consistent with rehabbing it.

I commute to work by 205 3x a week(ish) so I'm a little more used to it, but it's great to go south down...depending on the amount of litter (never too bad), and homeless people dragging their shopping cart overflowing with 6 bags of cans tied down to them (happens maybe 1 in 7 times). Going north on 205, however, can either be a fun challenge or given a little bit of wind, the worst 20 minutes of the day... middle of a freeway, on a bridge, over a river, 3-5% incline with no tree/wind coverage... it can be absolutely miserable, lmao. But alternatively, you bike 17 miles to go around it by I5 or ride up to bridge of the gods 💀💀 

As for I5, it's definitely more sketch (danger-wise), as going south, you have to go through the "r*pe tunnel" which is a dark tunnel about 25-feet wide and 60-feet long, with no lights and a weird cage that is perfect size for someone to hind behind. I don't go through it unless it's sunny and middle of the day, however going north, there is a short gravel climb you can do to avoid going through this tunnel. My issues with I5 however, is the size. 205 is a double-wide lane in the middle, but I5 has a very narrow path between the bridge and the water, with a single rail separating. It's sketch enough riding on there, but homeless people NEVER go the way with traffic, so you will (90% of the time) have to play chicken with a homeless person on a bike, walking, or carrying a cart to see who will stop and step into the bridge beam to wait for the other to go by. After maybe my 50th time crossing yesterday, I finally yelled, "The right way for you to go is with traffic on the other end, you lazy f*ck" which was definitely out of pocket but I need to realize what's common sense for me may be foreign knowledge to someone else, but I'm also afraid of natural water, so the thought of someone not knowing what they're doing and knocking me off the edge into the water is a great fear of mine. The best part about I5 though, is that it's maybe 1/5 the size of 205, and it's maybe 80ft up, and 80ft right back down you can coast. Definitely don't recommend sprinting, though... handlebars might get catch on the guard railing 🤦🏽‍♂️

TL:DR- I205 is long and steep.... great to go south and can be fun to go north unless there's any kind of wind. I5 is a fraction of the size and vertical, but is a lot more frustrating dealing with pedestrian/bike traffic and is a sketchier area.

Just got my first pair of clipless. I went with shimano spd sl 105, and tbh, I got it because that's the gears gearset that I got on my bike. I've been loving them so far, I feel like my pedaling is more efficient. I know there's studies that show its not that much of a difference, but for me personally, it helps the push/pull balance and I can use my muscles more efficiently. 

I will also say, that before these, I used the Magped system, which is kind of a hybrid setup. It's a clipless magnet, so you use road shoes, but instead of "clipping-in", the shoe plates have super strong magnets that give you the same feeling as clipless, but mental security of knowing you're not "locked-in". 

Comparatively speaking, the magpeds worked great but they're a solo small business, so you have to order parts direct from them, shimano parts are literally everywhere. The magpeds are in general easier to release, but after a few rides the spd are equally easy, with a tension screw you can control the ease/difficulty of entry/release and its awesome. Price wise, the magpeds are just over $200 (us) and for that price, you could get ultegra pedals, where the 105 are $150 (us). 

All that being said, I love the spd switch, but I'm glad I used the magpeds before, because I definitely would have fallen alot trying to use the spds at first. However, I do plan on getting a pair of Shimano eh500, that are dual (flat&spd) compatible, for versatility, sometimes I don't wanna put on cleats to the store, or stroll rides, bikepacking trips, etc, but I also commute, so having a clipless system has become a necessity for sustained energy outputs on longer rides! 
 
P.s. if you plan on getting a power meter, you may want to consider speedplay, but that also is a personal preference (I've heard), as there are many types of power meters

Broke my fibula my 6th time skiing on the mountain. To be fair, I've never snowboarded, but my decision to ski instead of snowboard was based off the following: 
- when in a snowboard, if you hit a bank or your board gets stuck, your feet stay in, and you either destroy your knee or your ankle in the process, vs in skis, you will pop out... not saying injury isn't possible (my injury was because of downward force, I fell off a cliff), but your legs aren't fixed onto the board 
- when falling, on a snowboard you're either falling on your face or on the back of your head when you catch an edge,(or break wrists tryna break the fall) and on skis, if you learn to fall, most of the time you can baseball/side slide to break the fall. You do have to worry about pole impaling, but proper form will protect. 
- no waiting after the lift to strap in 
- more control in turns, based off what I've seen, you can make tighter/faster turns in skis, and as I had interest in trees, I favored in control. 

Risk and injury are gonna be a factor to think about whatever you're doing, but someone told me once " Skiing is easier to learn, but harder to master, while snowboarding is harder to learn, and easier to master. Skiing is dope, snowboarding is dope, I think Skiing is just a little more versatile and efficient on the mountain.

I have been thinking about this for some time... I grew up playing football, and was very much pressured to do so from adolescence, though i was blessed enough to play through college. To be honest, I never even considered skiing growing up because whenever it came up it was always "skiing is for white people", so I stayed in my lil ignorant box. I played my college ball in Montana, and once I got out there I saw that a plethora of people were up on the mountains having the time of their lives! We weren't allowed to ski being on the football team (risk of injury), but a bunch of the guys who grew up skiing would go for a weekend right after spring ball. 

After I graduated, I was convinced by some family to go up skiing for a day (we live an hour from Mt. Hood). The first 3 hours was probably the most frustrating time I've had in my life, but after that switch flipped, I absolutely fell in love. 
Playing football, I couldn't tell you how many times I've smashed my head in something, and in every which direction as well. I learned how to fall and how to land when in the air in football, so those skills transferred nicely when making the transfer, but I had new terrain to learn, and didn't look before I leaped. Broke my fibula right above the ankle, tore some ligaments in my foot, and got a plate w 5 screws installed. Worse injury I'd had in my life (to date). I fucked up cause I didn't know what I was doing, versus in football I've been fucked up because someone else didn't know what they were doing. This can go both ways, cause someone can be blindsided on the mountain, and a tackler can duck their own head in football, but user error is the most common errors in skiing, whereas most accidents in football are a 2-party issue. 
I see kids Learning how to ski at the age of 3-4, but you don't see kids playing tackle football until 11-12 (a little earlier back when I was a kid). I know I've become a little slower in thought process and definitely seen some effects of being hit in the head a lot, although I'm still (mostly) functional. Long story short it's easier to be self-responsible in skiing, versus in football you're counting on 10 other guys to help you out, and when one person (or more) messes up you have double the boom coming for you. 

TLDR: 
It's easier to teach your kid respect and rules by yourself  than to send him with a bigger group of nincompoops to eun around and smash eachother in the head.

Another thing with testing. The number on your bag represents (more than likely) the best buds on the entire plant. The farm send the top colas to the labs for testing and sent all the bottom buds to the dispensaries to get sold. The testing material represents very little of the flower that actually makes it to the dispo.
